q: Who is the author of the story "The Midnight Visitor"?
o: Robert Arthur
Victor Canning
H. G. Wells
Guy de Maupassant
e: Robert Arthur wrote the suspense story "The Midnight Visitor" featuring secret agent Ausable.

q: Who wrote the story "A Question of Trust"?
o: James Herriot
Ruskin Bond
Robert Arthur
Victor Canning
e: British thriller writer Victor Canning authored "A Question of Trust", starring gentleman burglar Horace Danby.

q: In "The Midnight Visitor", who was Ausable?
o: A police inspector
A hotel waiter
A secret agent
A romantic writer
e: Ausable was an intelligent, quick-witted secret agent whose unassuming appearance surprised Fowler.

q: What was Horace Danby fond of collecting?
o: Antique clocks
Rare and expensive books
Gold coins
Oil paintings
e: Horace Danby loved rare, expensive books and robbed one safe every year to buy them secretly through an agent.

q: Who was Fowler in "The Midnight Visitor"?
o: The hotel manager
A young and romantic writer
A missile scientist
A rival spy
e: Fowler was a young and romantic writer who had come to meet Ausable hoping for thrilling espionage adventure.

q: What was Horace Danby's legitimate business profession?
o: Making locks
Police investigation
Selling books
Jewellery trading
e: Horace Danby made locks and ran a successful business with two helpers.

q: What did Max have in his hand inside Ausable's hotel room?
o: A sharp knife
A silver lighter
A passkey
A small automatic pistol
e: As Ausable switched on the light, Max stood halfway across the room holding a small automatic pistol pointed at them.

q: In "A Question of Trust", what was "Sherry"?
o: The young lady in red
Horace Danby's book agent
A small dog in the kitchen of Shotover Grange
The housekeeper at Shotover Grange
e: Sherry was the small friendly dog lying in the kitchen at Shotover Grange whom Horace calmed by calling his name.

q: On which floor of the French hotel was Ausable's room located?
o: Ground floor
Second floor
Sixth and top floor
Fourth floor
e: Ausable stayed in a small, musty room on the sixth and top floor of a gloomy French hotel in Paris.

q: What was the name of the big house that Horace Danby planned to rob in July?
o: Baskerville Hall
Shotover Grange
Windsor Manor
Oakridge Villa
e: For two weeks Horace had carefully studied Shotover Grange, its electric wiring, paths, and garden.

q: Which important document did Max come to take from Ausable?
o: A report concerning some new missiles
A railway timetable
A passport
A bank cheque
e: Max entered Ausable's room at pistol-point to seize a confidential report concerning new missiles.

q: What allergy troubled Horace Danby during the summer?
o: Cold wind allergy
Dust allergy
Seafood allergy
Hay fever triggered by flowers
e: Horace suffered from attacks of hay fever in summer, and the bowl of flowers in Shotover Grange made him sneeze loudly.

q: How did Max actually enter Ausable's hotel room?
o: Through a neighbouring balcony
Climbing a drainpipe
Hiding in a laundry cart
Using a passkey through the door
e: Max explicitly admits he knew nothing of any balcony and had entered the room with a passkey.

q: Approximately how old was Horace Danby, and what was his marital status?
o: Sixty years old and widowed
Twenty-five years old and married
About fifty years old and unmarried
Thirty years old and married
e: Horace Danby was about fifty years old, unmarried, and lived with a housekeeper who worried over his health.

q: Who actually knocked at Ausable's door near the end of "The Midnight Visitor"?
o: Max's secret accomplice
Henry the waiter bringing the ordered drink
Armed Paris police
The hotel owner
e: Though Ausable bluffed that it was the police, the visitor was simply Henry the waiter returning with a tray, a bottle, and two glasses.

q: How often did Horace Danby commit a robbery?
o: Every year once
Every month
Every week
Once in ten years
e: Horace robbed just one safe a year—stealing enough to last twelve months and buy rare books.

q: Where was Ausable originally from before coming to Paris twenty years earlier?
o: Boston
Berlin
New York
London
e: Although Ausable spoke French and German passably, he had never lost the American accent brought from Boston twenty years ago.

q: Where was the safe hidden inside the drawing room of Shotover Grange?
o: Behind the kitchen curtain
Under the fireplace carpet
Inside a wooden bookshelf
Behind a rather poor painting
e: The safe stood behind a rather poor painting in the drawing room—something even a magazine article had revealed.

q: What animal did Max's sharp facial features resemble according to the narrator?
o: A wolf
A bulldog
A fox
A panther
e: Max is described as slender, a little less than tall, with features suggesting the crafty, pointed countenance of a fox.

q: What colour outfit was the young, pretty woman at Shotover Grange wearing?
o: White
Red
Blue
Black
e: The clever young burglar who posed as the lady of the house was dressed completely in red.

q: How much worth of jewels were inside the Shotover Grange safe?
o: One thousand pounds
About fifteen thousand pounds
Five hundred pounds
Fifty thousand pounds
e: There were about fifteen thousand pounds' worth of jewels in the safe, from which Horace hoped to fetch at least five thousand.

q: What surprised Ausable's guest Fowler right as they entered the dark room?
o: Seeing a man with a small automatic pistol standing halfway across the room
Seeing secret maps on the wall
Hearing sirens outside the window
Finding the room ransacked
e: Feeling disappointed until then, Fowler experienced his "first authentic thrill of the day" seeing Max pointing a pistol.

q: What was Horace Danby's role in prison at the end of "A Question of Trust"?
o: Chief lockmaker
Garden supervisor
Head cook
Assistant librarian
e: Just as during his first sentence fifteen years earlier, Horace now works as the assistant librarian in the prison.

q: How did Ausable convince Max that there was a balcony outside his window?
o: He opened the curtains to display it
He showed him architectural blueprints
He grumbled angrily that it was the second time someone had entered via the next room's balcony
He pointed to footprints on the window ledge
e: With natural frustration, Ausable invented a detailed complaint about the hotel management failing to block off the neighbouring balcony.

q: Why was Horace Danby arrested by noon on the third day after the robbery?
o: Sherry barked and led police to him
The servants returned early from the cinema
His fingerprints were found all over the drawing room after he removed his gloves
He tried to sell the jewels to a policeman
e: After removing his gloves to light the lady's cigarette and open the safe bare-handed, Horace left clear fingerprints everywhere.

q: For which time was Ausable's appointment with the missile report scheduled?
o: Two a.m.
Twelve-thirty
Eight o'clock
Ten-fifteen
e: Ausable murmured moodily, "Thirty-one minutes... The appointment was for twelve-thirty."

q: Who actually lived in the house at Shotover Grange while Horace robbed it?
o: In London
At the cinema
In Paris
In the kitchen
e: The family who owned Shotover Grange was away in London, leaving only two servants in charge—who went to the movies.

q: What did Max do when the doorknob turned while he stood on the windowsill?
o: He shot at the door
He hid under Ausable's bed
He handed back the pistol
He pushed away from the sill to drop onto the imaginary balcony and screamed shrilly
e: Panicked by the turning doorknob and thinking armed police were entering, Max dropped straight from the sixth-floor window screaming shrilly.

q: What common saying makes Horace Danby get "very angry" at the end of the story?
o: "Look before you leap"
"Time and tide wait for none"
"All that glitters is not gold"
"Honour among thieves"
e: Having been outwitted and betrayed by a fellow thief in red, Horace gets furious whenever anyone mentions "honour among thieves."

q: Where had Ausable and Fowler spent a "dull evening" before returning to the hotel?
o: At a London restaurant
At a secret bunker
At a French music hall
In a crowded railway station
e: Ausable jokingly sympathized with Fowler for spending "a dull evening in a French music hall with a sloppy fat man."

q: What physical details made Ausable look completely unlike a typical fictional spy?
o: He wore dark sunglasses and carried a sword
He was very fat, sloppy, wheezed while walking, and spoke with an American Boston accent
He walked with a limp and carried books
He was tall, muscular, and silent
e: Fowler noticed Ausable didn't fit any spy stereotype: he was fat, wheezy, lived in a drab room, and kept his Boston accent.

q: How did Horace Danby first learn that Shotover Grange had a safe hidden behind a painting?
o: A magazine article had published a description, room plan, and picture of the drawing room
He guessed by tapping on every wall
His two helpers had repaired the safe earlier
The housekeeper told him at the market
e: Horace mused on how foolish wealthy owners are: the writer of a magazine article had printed the room plan and mentioned the safe behind the painting.

q: What specific detail did Ausable invent about the history of the room next door?
o: That his room was once part of a larger unit and the next room used to be the living room with a balcony
That Henry the waiter slept in that room
That a famous burglar used to rent it
That the French police rented the room next door
e: To sound realistic, Ausable explained that the room next door was formerly the living room whose balcony extended under his window from an empty room two doors down.

q: When did Horace Danby serve his first and only prison sentence before the Shotover Grange case?
o: Five years ago
Twenty-five years ago
Two years ago
Fifteen years ago
e: The narrator reveals that fifteen years ago Horace had served his first and only sentence in a prison library.

q: What made Ausable say Fowler had "spent a dull evening" instead of seeing spies and beauties?
o: Because the French music hall caught fire
Because Fowler forgot his notebook at home
Because instead of gunshots, drugged wine, and messages from dark-eyed beauties, Ausable only got a prosaic phone call
Because Ausable lost his secret phone number
e: Ausable playfully mocked Fowler's romantic thriller expectations—explaining that real espionage mostly involves ordinary appointments and dull waiting.

q: How many hours did Horace Danby have before the servants returned from the movies?
o: Six hours
Four hours
One hour
Two hours
e: After arriving at the drawing room, Horace laid out his tools carefully, noting he had four hours before the servants returned.

q: What did Ausable say when Max threatened to wait outside on the balcony until the "police" left?
o: That the balcony was newly painted
That the police wouldn't wait—the door was unlocked and they wouldn't hesitate to shoot
That Fowler would lock the window from inside
That Max could take the missile report right now
e: Ausable calmly turned the pressure up: "The door is unlocked. And they will not hesitate to shoot," forcing Max out onto the sill before Henry entered.

q: What three specific rare items or books did Horace want to buy in autumn with the Shotover Grange loot?
o: Three very interesting books coming up for sale in the autumn
Four antique lock sets
Five paintings for his living room
Two diamond rings and a coat
e: Horace calculated that five thousand pounds from the fifteen-thousand-pound jewels would let him buy three very interesting books coming up for sale in autumn.

q: What had Ausable actually ordered earlier that evening before bringing Fowler up to his room?
o: Extra blankets for the sixth floor
Coffee and French bread
Hot soup and sandwiches
A drink (a bottle and two glasses) to be brought when he returned
e: Before meeting Max, Ausable had already instructed Henry the waiter to bring up a bottle and two glasses once he returned to his room.

q: Where had the housekeeper left the kitchen door key at Shotover Grange?
o: Under a flowerpot
Inside the mailbox
Hanging on a hook outside the kitchen door
With the gardener
e: Horace had watched the housekeeper hang the kitchen door key on a hook outside—making his gloved entry silent and effortless.

q: How did Ausable explain the sudden knock at the door to keep Max panicked?
o: He said it was Fowler's angry editor
He warned that Max's own boss had arrived
He claimed he had asked the police to check on him for extra protection of the important report
He said it was the hotel manager checking passports
e: With complete poise, Ausable smiled and claimed he thought an important missile paper needed extra police protection.

q: Why did Horace Danby cut a wire in the hall before working on the safe?
o: To cut the fireplace lamp
To disable the poorly built burglar alarm
To turn off the kitchen stove
To disconnect the television
e: Noting the burglar alarm was poorly built, Horace went into the hall and cut its wire before returning to sneeze loudly at the flowers.

q: How did Fowler's opinion of Ausable change from the start of the story to the very end?
o: From disappointment at his dull, fat appearance to stunned awe at his brilliant presence of mind
From admiration to intense anger
From fear to suspicion of crime
From friendship to complete boredom
e: Fowler started feeling let down by the unglamorous fat agent, but ended white-faced and stunned when Ausable calmly outwitted an armed spy without firing a shot.

q: What did the young lady in red ask Horace Danby to do before she let him leave without calling the police?
o: Return the kitchen key to the gardener
Drive her car to London
Repair her broken wristwatch
Break open the safe so she could get the jewels she needed for a party that night
e: Claiming she forgot the safe's combination and wanted to wear her jewels to a party tonight, she tricked Horace into breaking open the safe bare-handed.

q: Why couldn't Max keep his balance safely while escaping onto the supposed balcony?
o: Fowler threw a heavy bottle at him
Ausable pushed him out with a chair
The window glass broke under his weight
He kept his body twisted to aim his gun inside, then pushed off the sill onto empty air six floors up
e: Max never turned around to check outside because he kept his pistol aimed at Ausable and Fowler; pushing off the sill, he dropped straight to nothingness.

q: How did the young lady make Horace Danby take off his gloves without making him suspicious?
o: She ordered him to wash his hands in the kitchen
She threw red paint on his gloves
She casually took a cigarette from a silver box, making Horace remove his gloves to offer his lighter eagerly
She said gloves scared Sherry
e: Eager to please her so she would let him go, Horace impulsively pulled off his gloves to hold out his cigarette lighter—sealing his own arrest.

q: How did Ausable reveal at the very end that Max would not climb back from the balcony?
o: By telling Henry to lock the window
By sighing calmly, "No, he won't return. You see, my young friend, there is no balcony."
By telephoning the police downstairs
By showing a parachute on the bed
e: When white-faced Fowler asked "But won't that man out on the balcony...?", Ausable dropped the punchline: "there is no balcony."

q: Why did the young lady claim her husband would not notice the broken safe right away?
o: She claimed her husband wouldn't return for a month and she would have the safe mended before then
She claimed they owned ten safes in London
She said her husband was blind
She said her husband hated jewels
e: Reassuring Horace cleanly, she lied that her husband wouldn't return from London for a month, giving her ample time to mend the broken safe.

q: How long did Ausable tell Max it would take before the missile report arrived at his room?
o: Thirty-one minutes
Five minutes
Two hours
Midnight sharp
e: Closing his eyes thoughtfully, Ausable said moodily, "Thirty-one minutes. The appointment was for twelve-thirty."

q: How did the real wife of Shotover Grange's owner appear compared to the young lady in red?
o: Both were young and twenty-five
The real wife was a gray-haired, sharp-tongued woman of sixty, whereas the con artist was young and pretty
The real wife lived in Paris
The real wife wore the exact same red dress
e: When Horace told police the owner's wife asked him to open the safe, the real wife—a gray-haired, sharp-tongued woman of sixty—dismissed his story as nonsense.

q: Why did Ausable decide to get Max's threat permanently ended rather than just calling out loudly?
o: Because Henry the waiter wasn't armed and Max held a loaded automatic pistol aimed at both Ausable and Fowler
Because Ausable wanted Fowler to write a tragedy
Because Max was deaf
Because the telephone line was broken
e: Facing a ruthless armed intruder in a locked room, Ausable knew physical fighting was impossible for him, so he used psychological deception instead.

q: What did Horace Danby first think of doing when he realized the red painting hid the safe and wondered about collecting pictures instead of books?
o: To steal the painting too
To sell his lock business and open a gallery
To leave the jewels untouched
That books were better in a small house where there wasn't room for paintings
e: Even mid-burglary, Horace paused thoughtfully for a second before deciding books suited his small home far better than paintings.

q: When did Fowler hear "Max screamed once, shrilly"?
o: When Henry uncorked the bottle
Before Ausable opened the door
The moment Max pushed with his left hand from the windowsill to drop onto the nonexistent balcony
Right after the pistol misfired
e: As the doorknob turned, Max swung off the sill expecting a solid balcony beneath him and plunged six storeys with a single shrill scream.

q: How long did Horace Danby keep his promise to the young lady before planning his next robbery?
o: Twelve hours
Two days, and on the morning of the third day he thought of the books
Six months
One whole year
e: Horace kept his promise for two days, but on the third morning he remembered the autumn books and needed money—only to be arrested by noon.

q: How did Max react when Ausable said, "I thought you were in Berlin"?
o: He apologized and dropped his gun
He stood motionless halfway across the room, his small automatic pistol pointed steadily at Ausable and Fowler
He hid behind the curtains
He laughed and hugged Ausable
e: Even though Ausable greeted Max with casual coolness ("You gave me quite a start"), Max kept his gun trained steadily across the room.

q: How long did it take Horace Danby to break open the Shotover Grange safe for the lady in red?
o: Within an hour
Nearly four hours
All night
Ten minutes
e: Being a skilled lockmaker who had lived with locks and safes all his life, Horace opened it cleanly within an hour.

q: Why was Ausable waiting patiently inside his hotel room with his eyes closed right before the knock?
o: He was dizzy from Max's threats
He had fallen asleep due to exhaustion
He was praying for rescue
He was calm and mentally timing Henry the waiter's arrival to spring the police bluff on Max
e: Knowing he had ordered a drink from Henry before coming upstairs, Ausable remained cool, composed, and ready to exploit the knock.

q: What polite gesture did the housekeeper usually perform at home to care for Horace Danby?
o: She helped him steal rare books
She locked him inside his library
She worried over his health
She taught him to pick safes
e: Horace lived quietly as a respectable bachelor lockmaker with a housekeeper who constantly worried over his health and summer hay fever.

q: What did Ausable say Max had actually wanted when he demanded the paper "quietly"?
o: He wanted to burn the report
He wanted to sell it to Henry
He said the report concerning new missiles was in safer hands with him than with Ausable
He wanted to publish it in a newspaper
e: Max smoothly threatened that he would take the missile report "tonight" because "it will be in safer hands in mine than in yours."

q: What did the young lady claim she had promised her husband before leaving for London?
o: To paint over the drawing room safe
To take her jewels to their bank
To sell Shotover Grange
To dismiss the two servants
e: To explain why she wanted the jewels out secretly without calling police, she fabricated a story of forgetting the safe numbers after failing to put the jewels in the bank.

q: Read the extract: "Ausable did not fit any description of a secret agent Fowler had ever read." What misconception of Fowler does this expose?
o: He expected all spies to be slim, glamorous, fearless action heroes instead of ordinary-looking, sharp-minded men
He thought secret agents must carry textbooks
He believed spies live only in London mansions
He thought spies cannot speak English
e: Fowler judged intelligence by outer glamour and physique, failing at first to see that real espionage thrives on calm intellect rather than theatrical looks.

q: Read the line: "Everyone thought that Horace Danby was a good, honest citizen." Why is the narrator quick to add "but not completely honest"?
o: Because he lied about his age to the housekeeper
Because he never paid his two helpers
Because Horace cheated customers on lock prices
Because behind his respectable lockmaker life, he broke open a rich safe once every year to fund his passion for rare books
e: Horace lived peacefully without violence and stole only once a year from the rich, creating a polite double life that wasn't truly honest.

q: What does the word "countenance" mean in "his features suggested slightly the crafty, pointed countenance of a fox"?
o: Weapon holster
Clothing style
Accent of speech
Face or facial expression
e: "Countenance" means a person's face or facial expression, highlighting Max's sly, fox-like sharpness.

q: Why was the young lady in red able to control Sherry the dog and adjust the fireplace ornaments so convincingly?
o: Because she was actually the housekeeper's daughter
She carried dog biscuits in her pocket
She had carefully prepared her act—researching the house and dog's name—to impersonate the lady of the manor flawlessly
She threatened Sherry with a whistle
e: Just like Horace had studied Shotover Grange for two weeks, the rival thief had learned Sherry's name and practiced calm aristocratic authority.

q: What does the word "prosaic" mean in "gets only a prosaic telephone call making an appointment"?
o: Coded in German
Dull, ordinary, and lacking romantic excitement
Violent and threatening
Mysterious and dangerous
e: "Prosaic" describes something commonplace and unexciting—Ausable uses it humorously to contrast drab reality with thriller fiction.

q: What insight about Horace Danby's character is revealed by his hesitation over stealing books vs stealing money from rich people's safes?
o: He convinced himself his white-collar burglary was cultured and harmless rather than violent crime
He stole only to pay for his helpers' weddings
He hated reading and sold books illegally
He wanted to become famous in newspapers
e: Horace rationalized stealing once a year as a refined hobby for a cultured gentleman—blind to the fact that crime always rests on risk and deceit.

q: Why did Ausable NOT look worried or nervous when he saw Max pointing a pistol at him?
o: His long experience as a secret agent kept him composed, allowing his quick brain to immediately craft the balcony trap
Because Ausable had a bulletproof vest on
Because he recognized Max as an old school friend
Because he saw the pistol had no bullets
e: Years of espionage trained Ausable to conceal panic; his casual tone ("You gave me quite a start") instantly threw Max off guard.

q: In "A Question of Trust", what does the phrase "How foolish people are when they own valuable things" tell us about Horace's mindset?
o: Anger toward magazine editors
Fear of getting hay fever
Concern for public safety at Shotover Grange
Overconfidence in his own cleverness right before he himself gets tricked far worse
e: Notice the dramatic irony: Horace mocks wealthy homeowners for careless publicity just minutes before blindly trusting a complete stranger in red.

q: Why did Max believe Ausable's balcony story so readily without verifying it?
o: Because the moonlight lit up the balcony railing
Because Max had stayed in that exact room last month
Because Ausable complained naturally about the hotel management rather than boasting, making it sound like an ordinary irritation
Because Fowler confirmed he had climbed up that balcony
e: Ausable didn't say "look at that balcony"; he vented annoyingly about "the second time in a month" and management promises—convincing Max immediately.

q: What does the lady mean when she tells Horace, "I have always liked the wrong kind of people"?
o: She genuinely wanted to marry Horace
She flattered and disarmed his fear of prison so he would lower his guard and gladly obey her request
She was confessing she worked for the police
She hated Shotover Grange's servants
e: Her charming smile and playful sympathy manipulated Horace into feeling safe, grateful, and eager to please her—even to the point of removing his gloves.

q: What did Fowler mean when he felt "the first authentic thrill of the day" upon seeing Max?
o: He enjoyed French music halls immensely
Finally encountering real armed danger matched the exciting spy world he had hoped to write about
He wanted to buy an automatic pistol
He loved the decor of Ausable's sixth-floor hotel room
e: Up to that moment, Fowler felt bored and let down by Ausable's ordinary evening; suddenly facing a real gunman turned dullness into genuine suspense.

q: Why didn't the police believe Horace Danby's truthful explanation that the lady of the house told him to open the safe?
o: Because the real wife was a sharp-tongued sixty-year-old woman who proved Horace's story absurd against his fingerprints everywhere
Because the two servants testified they saw Horace alone
Because Horace refused to reveal his lockmaking shop address
Because no safe was ever broken at Shotover Grange
e: Every physical trace belonged only to Horace—and the real elderly mistress naturally denied ever asking a stranger to break open her safe.

q: Read Ausable's opening words: "You are disappointed... You were told that I was a secret agent, a spy..." What does this reveal about Ausable's personality?
o: He was angry at Fowler for staring at him
He disliked his own profession as a secret agent
He wanted Fowler to leave the hotel before midnight
He had sharp, perceptive empathy and could immediately read Fowler's unstated disillusionment
e: Ausable quietly senses Fowler's letdown without being told—showing the observant psychological awareness that makes him a master agent.

q: In "A Question of Trust", what does the word "hindrance" mean in the context of Horace's hay fever?
o: A rare book title
A secret entrance
An obstacle or obstruction interfering with his work
Helpful protection
e: Hay fever proved a fatal "hindrance" (obstacle) to Horace's quiet burglary—his loud sneezes alerted the burglar in red to his exact spot.

q: Why did Max say, "It might have saved me some trouble had I known" about the supposed balcony?
o: Max worked as a hotel repairman
Max actually lost his passkey in the lobby
Using an outside balcony would have seemed easier than obtaining a passkey—showing Max completely swallowed Ausable's bait
Max wanted to admire the view of Paris
e: Max's remark confirms to Ausable that his bluff worked 100%: Max now treats the nonexistent balcony as an established escape route.

q: What role did the "pretty young lady in red" use to gain absolute psychological authority over Horace Danby?
o: A detective from Scotland Yard
The calm, firm mistress of Shotover Grange returning unexpectedly from London
Horace's book dealer's assistant
A magazine reporter writing about locks
e: Combining a "quiet, kindly voice, yet with firmness," calling Sherry by name, and tidying ornaments established total domestic authority.

q: In "The Midnight Visitor", what does Ausable's casual request to Henry—"Just set the tray on the table. Uncork the bottle, and leave the room"—prove about his nerves?
o: He wasn't even rattled moments after eliminating a dangerous armed spy through sheer wit
He was angry with Henry for arriving late
He didn't realize Max had dropped
He wanted to celebrate with Max outside
e: While Fowler sat pale and trembling, Ausable calmly turned back to hospitality as if nothing extraordinary had occurred.

q: Why did the young lady ask Horace to get his tools ready only AFTER taking the silver cigarette box?
o: She planned to hide jewels in the silver box
She needed a smoke to relieve her cough
She wanted to reward Horace with expensive tobacco
Offering a cigarette cleverly tricked him into taking off his gloves so he would leave fingerprints on everything
e: From start to finish, the cigarette scene was a calculated move to strip off Horace's gloves and shift all forensic blame onto him.

q: What irony lies in Max saying "Wait outside until they go, or I'll shoot and take my chances"?
o: His gun actually fired blank bullets
Fowler secretly caught him on the ledge
The police really were waiting downstairs
By believing he was choosing a safe hiding place on the "balcony" to avoid imaginary police, he blindly stepped to his own doom
e: Max thought he held all the cards with his pistol, yet Ausable directed him straight out of a sixth-floor window through pure psychological coercion.

q: Why did Victor Canning mention right at the start that Horace Danby had served a sentence in a "prison library"?
o: To prove Horace stole his first books from prison
To warn readers against working in libraries
To hint that Horace already knew prison life inside books and ironically ended up back as an assistant prison librarian at the end
To show Horace wanted to become a judge
e: The opening mention of a prison library creates a full narrative circle when Horace finishes the story working as assistant librarian in prison.

q: Which quality helped Ausable defeat Max despite having no weapon of his own?
o: Luck when Max tripped over a suitcase
Presence of mind, cool temperament, and brilliant improvisation under pressure
Physical strength and judo skills
Help from armed Paris police
e: Ausable turned two mundane things—an empty window and a waiter's scheduled room delivery—into an unbeatable psychological weapon.

q: What fatal mistake turned Horace Danby from a careful, seasoned burglar into an easy suspect?
o: Underestimating a fellow thief posing as an innocent woman and removing his protective gloves
Forgetting to cut the burglar alarm wire
Leaving his bag of tools on the garden path
Calling the police himself
e: Despite two weeks of meticulous planning, one chivalrous moment without gloves left Horace's fingerprints all over the drawing room and safe.

q: When Ausable sighed moodily, "I wish I knew how you learned about the report, Max," what effect did his remark have on the confrontation?
o: Ausable murmured it calmly to unsettle Max and show he treated the intrusion coolly without panic
Fowler yelled it at Max from the door
Henry asked it while carrying the tray
Max asked Fowler to learn Ausable's secrets
e: Ausable calmly reversed the interrogation, making Max feel scrutinized rather than in complete command of the situation.

q: What did the young lady's words—"Society must be protected from men like you"—reveal when viewed in hindsight?
o: She planned to donate the jewels to a library
She was actually a secret judge
She genuinely hated all thieves and returned the jewels to London
She lectured Horace on morality while smoothly committing the exact same jewel theft herself!
e: Preaching high-minded civic morality to a cornered burglar while robbing the same safe proves her cold-blooded brilliance as a con artist.

q: Why did Ausable NOT tell Fowler beforehand that Henry the waiter would knock shortly?
o: Because Ausable had forgotten he ordered a drink
Because Henry arrived three hours early
Fowler's genuine shock at the sudden knock made the "police" bluff completely authentic and convincing to Max
Because Ausable distrusted Fowler
e: Fowler jumped involuntarily when the loud knock sounded—providing unscripted dramatic proof that convinced Max the police had arrived.

q: How does Horace's preparation for robbing Shotover Grange contrast with his reaction to the lady in red?
o: He planned to meet the lady all along
He planned every mechanical lock and wire logically, yet melted emotionally under mild fear and charm
He grew angry and fought the servants
He forgot to bring any burglary tools
